blocks.x: You can just give your names or we can always identify.
But I mean, now what do you want me to talk about? I thought you were going to ask me.
No, you can just give your name first.
I, Edward B. Garland.
When were you born?
Well, I was born January the 9th, 1895.
Right in New Orleans?
In New Orleans, yeah.
Do you remember which street or part of town?
Yes, I do. Right where the old Paris prison is. That's on Basin Street, which is called Saratoga. That's right between Tulane and Gravia. Right in front of the Paris prison before it was there.
And what was that year again? 18?
So you're a little older than Fess then, about four years. I was going to ask while I think of it, that name Montutti, where did you ever get that name?

Well, I got that name. I'll tell you what we got that name. We used to play in the cafe, you know, nightclub. And this old guy used to come to hear us play. Pretty nice thought. He'd give us lots of tips, you know. And that was his name. They called him Montutti. Well, I was learning that name Montutti is called Duke. I don't know. Well, anyhow, O'Re and the boys, all this stuff. When the guy come in late, they say, come on there, old Montutti. You look just like Montutti. Well, they'd laugh at all. Johnny does, they just laugh. Render Stahls, he'd laugh. All of them would laugh. And when he'd say it to me, I'd get angry about it. You see? So when they found out that that was my goat, you know, they kept it up. I would be on a bandstand at Howard. I don't know, Montutti, but when I turned around to... First, it was Lorenzo or some of them. The guys don't know they ain't at Howard, man. They had me all night looking from one side to another, you know. So they just kept on saying Montutti, and I just told them that I was going to... There was going to be trouble when they stopped calling me that name. Finally, they kept calling to me so much, I answered one night. I forgot all about it. And from there on, that was it. Montutti. And they've been calling me Montutti for many years.

That's what they call Fess Hoss. Yeah. They all call him Fess now. Yeah. Can you remember the earliest music you ever heard when you were a boy? Was it on the parades or in the churches or at home? Anybody at home playing? Well, my brother, yeah.
Is he an older brother?
Yeah. What was his name? John Garland.

Is he still living? That's what I'm telling you about. That's what I don't know. I just mail, fixed the mail of that again. I got a letter from him saying he was very little sick, you know, in Philadelphia. 642 North 47th Street, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. And I haven't gotten no answer. That's what I've been waiting on to answer.
Is that within a few months that you heard from him?
This year, not like a couple of weeks ago.
A couple of weeks ago? Yes. Quite sick.
That's what they say.
They live on 47th Street in Philadelphia. In Philadelphia.
He was an older brother.
That's the oldest one, yeah.
Only had one brother, the sister. Ain't nobody living but just he and I. Yes.
What did he play? Well, Johnny, you know Johnny, don't you?
Well, I certainly know Johnny. He was a violin player. He played violin player? That's right. He played violin and he played trombone. He played mandolin. Sure. Guitar.
About how much older was he than you? It was four years apart. Four years. I mean, two years apart. Two years apart, you see.
Two years between me and my sister. Two years between my sister and him.
Did your father and mother play anything or sing?
No, I don't know about my mother singing or nothing because I think I was four years old. No, my mother passed.
Do you remember any music in the churches when you were young? Which church did you belong to?
Yeah, I remember music in church. Music. I used to go to St. James Church. The church called St. James Church. That was on Roman and between Iberville and Bienville.
Was that a Catholic church?
Well, that was a Methodist church. But I used to attend to St. Catholic Church regularly. I did.
Were you a Catholic then?
I was, yeah. But I used to go to this church with my friends.
That's right on Tuesday.

You know how kids go. They had to go to church every Sunday night and Sunday, especially Sunday school. And I'd go along with them besides going over to St. Catholic Church. I didn't like to go to church with them, you know. Yeah. The gang. But I used to be around called a Cuddy all the time. That's pretty good view of a party, Cuddy. Sure. That's in Captains. Yeah. That's in me. Right. We used to play us in Captains Hall. Oh yes.
I've heard of that.
Yeah.
Can you remember the earliest bands you ever heard or parades or what kind of music, dance music or any kind that you heard that way when you were a boy?

Oh, when I was a boy, I used to hear the old salsa band, you know. No, I don't know. Oh yeah, and this band Cross the River. Pacific? Pacific band, brass band, you know. The old time band. I was trying to call it the older bands, you know. The Armaged Band, you see. Well, I mean like an orchestra, I see.
Are you speaking of Robin? Any kind of music at all? Grass bands or orchestras? Do you remember some of the early orchestras you heard when you were really young?

Oh yeah, all the orchestras. We were only coming down to the orchestras in my younger days. And the band I always was crazy about was the Imperial Band and the Imperial, what was it? The Imperial Band, yeah. You know? Because, well I was pretty good sized then because I used to a lot of time pinch it for Brown. Oh yes. Used to play bass. James Brown was that his name?
What was his name, Brown?
He died basically. Jimmy Brown. Jimmy Brown, that's his name. And Oak Gasper and the Imperial Band.
Well can you tell us, when you first took up music, did you start on bass or any other instrument? What was your first instrument? Guitar. Oh yeah.

I was messing around with my brother, had all the minstrels laying around and I used to play a few little numbers on the mandolin, you know. I liked guitar, you know, for a while, but it always was for me to be a bass player. Did you take any lessons on it or did he show you? He did. I didn't take any kind of lessons. I just picked it up, you understand, and with him showing me. I didn't take no kind of lessons until I got to Chicago. I didn't know nothing about that.
About reading music until you got to Chicago.
In Chicago and I had an old man Jackson. Dave Payton's a man that told me, you go to Dave Jackson and take you some lessons. Well he used to have the band in the Grand Theater.
Oh yes, I knew some of the people that studied with him too. How old were you when you started on the guitar, would you say?
In fact, when I started out, I was around nine years old. When did you have a bass? I really was around ten years old. I was playing a little bass. Already on bass?
Yeah. Did your brother have a bass or did you have a little violin?
Yeah, my brother had a bass, yeah. My brother had a bass. He had a bass, guitar, mandolin, violin, taboo, and he had all those things.
Do you remember how many strings that bass had? Was it four or three?
No, three strings. Three. Three strings.
How did you tune that three string bass?
A, D, G. E, D, G.
A, D, G. A, D, G. Left off the lowest one.
Left off the E.
Yeah, the big one.

And when I learned how to finger E string, I was, the man who learned me how to play a four-string bass was Andrew Kimball. Oh, yeah. Henry Kimball. Henry Kimball. Henry Kimball. Henry Kimball, Robichaud's bass player. And you may believe it or not, I was the oldest one who could go sit in Robichaud's band and play. Robichaud didn't allow that, you know, those certain days, them guys, you know.
No, no, I guess it wasn't allowed.
No, but Andrew was screwing me and he showed me how to, see, we just bought it bass and we'll take that E string off. Oh, make it free string on it.
Take the E string off.
We couldn't figure out what that string was going on. Take it off. And then you put that string on. And you ought to make these pedal notes on that string. You need it.
Oh, were you bowing then mostly or picking?

Bowing, bowing mostly. Bowing, bowing, bowing. Oh, boy. Wasn't doing the picking, I was doing the bowing. So, bow break down, we used to buy a spool of number eight thread and make me a thread of my own bow, a thread. Like a thread, number eight.
Put it right on that bow.
But then that bowing, you put a lot of that old pulverized razzle water, we go up a razzle plant and pick up a big piece of razzle. Part it, put it all over there, it'd go right on.
Who was the first person you ever heard pick on that bass? Can you remember?
Well, all I can tell you, I don't know who was the first to pick. It looked like it's just one of them things that looked like it just come up to all of us. See, from the pizzicata, you know.
Yeah.

The pizzicata, there you see, this thing here. But the father starts picking, you know. Bowies, many times we break our bow and we just go ahead and pick. Yeah. And they just automatically come to us and start to pick them.
Yeah, sure. People in the symphony artists, they always pick in the symphony artists. Yeah. That's pizzicata, that is, yeah.
But that slap in the bass, that's how that come up.
Mm-hmm.

You do something, we come along and see you do something. That was all we'd do it. Yeah. Just like we all be playing. We get to playing, you understand. Fetch up, be playing a number on his violin. Somewhere we hear it. That's all. We go back, that cat would whistle it to him. I'd go, doo, doo, doo, doo, doo, doo, doo. That was all. We had it. Yeah.
That's how we got it. Who would you say is the best bass player of those old timers when you were young? Who would be your favorite, do you think? Or do you have a favorite, or did you?

Well, it was, oh, we had, let me see, Sam. Sam Nixon. Huh? Sam Nixon. Sam Nixon. Sam Nixon was a pretty good bass player. Yeah. Oak Gospel. Yeah. Well, my bass to leave for as far as I, in my book was, Henry Kimball was Thompson. See? Well, he was an actor, good musician, reason everything, you know. Jimmy Brown was a good bass player. Oh, yeah. Yeah.
Do you remember, was Jimmy Johnson older than you? I guess he was.

Oh, yeah. Jimmy, Jimmy, Jimmy Johnson, yeah, I used to sing. Oh, sure, we all met him. Sure. Of course. Jimmy Johnson, well, he played all right. He used to play with Jack Carey, you know. He played with the Crescent Band, you know. I love the Crescent Band. Yeah, and before he played with the Crescent Band, he used to play with, um. Play with Bolden. Buddy Bolden. Buddy Bolden.
Did you ever hear Bolden's band, that's one year?

Oh, yeah, Buddy Bolden's band. You played with him? Sure, I played with Jimmy, sure, and Jimmy. Jimmy used to work in some, uh, factory, you know. Factory, yeah. See? Bunch of factory. That's right. And lots of time, you know, he'd be late if he couldn't make it, and I used to pitch it for him. Yeah. He was playing at a hall on Padilla and Liberty called, uh, Kenny's Hall. Oh, yeah. You remember that, Kenny's Hall? That's a good one. I don't know.
I used to call it funky butthole. That's it.
I took a picture of it.
I took a picture of it.
That's all night, Saturday night or Sunday morning, and then twenty minutes after it'd be a church.
They turned it into a church, finally got a steeple on it, and church windows, you know.

Well, that's what it was after we, old man, old man all the time. But you'd play a dance and then they'd have church on Sunday. Yeah, you'd play Saturday night, they'd dance there, and see. They used it for church? And they used it for Sunday for the church. Oh, I didn't know that. Old man Kenny would own the place. Then the outfathers hall was running down there on Padilla and the ramparts. Padilla and the Rampart. Smith was at that. Yeah, and Kenny's Hall was on Liberty and Padilla. Different class of people. It was awful. Yeah, and Buddy Bowling used to play in there. I can tell you, every band played in a band.
Yeah, who else was it?

Buddy Bowling, trumpet. A fella named Frank played clarinet. Frank Lewis. Frank Lewis. Frank Lewis. All right, old Connish played trombone. Willie Connish played trombone. Jimmy Johnson played bass. James Phillips played drums. James Phillips. Yeah, he was out of his mouth in his mouth all the time. Two thing that, he'd go to sleep, get on the bandstand, wouldn't be there, and ten minutes before he'd go to bed. All the time. All the time.
And his name was Lewis? No, Jimmy Phillips.
Jimmy Phillips. Oh, Jimmy Phillips.
Yeah. Jimmy Phillips. Or Lewis was the clarinet.

Yeah. That's the way that was. Then Vien, Vien taking his place after that. Well, you remember when D.D. played with? D.D. Yeah, D.D. Channel. Yeah. Remember when D.D. played with? Sure. Remember when D.D. played with? Sure. Remember when D.D. played with? Sure. Remember when I played violin, when Frank had it? I remember that. Frank Duesen? Frank Duesen. Well, they had D.D. then. Yeah. And they had Frank Duesen. Even John Vien played with him, too. John Vien played with him after? After, yeah. And all the good drummers.
And you remember the very first job you ever played with? Yes, yes, I do. What was that?

I played a job and I, it was Caniniis Jackson. You love to go Caniniis Jackson? Caniniis Jackson played violin. While in the bass guitar? While in the bass. While in the bass. Well, he was playing guitar. My brother had to be on the bass. And John was playing his violin. Just three of us. A little house party. On Saturday night. What kind of a party? Just a little house party. A little house party.
A little house party.

A little fish fry or a house party? No, no, no, no. For a lawn party or anything? No, some people give a dance. Young kids, you know. They hired a band. You know. And Bruce said, I'm going to take you on the job tonight. Well, you see, 9 o'clock I had to be home. I had to be inside. Go to bed. And when that 9 o'clock come up, you know, that was it. He had me on that job. 9 o'clock come up again and get the drivers in. Sand make up. You know. I said, John, I can't. I'm sleepy. I can't play no more. I'm sleepy, you know. And everybody was standing around there looking. Looking at me, you see. I had no bass to have. I used to have the bass and I lay it halfway on my shoulder. You know. Played it. See. Yeah. of dancing and just watching me. Yeah. So I got sleeping. He up with his eyes and all that. That didn't make it. So I said, let the little fella sleep. He said, sit there and let him sit there and give him a little rest. Leave him sleep a while. So he told me to sit over there in the corner. Just guitar and violin played, you know. Well, I don't know, freshen up, you understand. Went on back to the bass and gigs, started to play it. I ain't never knew how much money I got, if I ever got it or not. But I do know how I played that carol, I'm so glad, you know. And I think I went somewhere just out free, you know, with Johnny, just going out having a good time. Next thing you know I was down in Hamburg, I used to go, I always run with older fellas than myself. I ran for the deed and that broke it up, you understand. I'd slip in them dances, you know, like the Oddfellas Hall and I'd play for Danny Lewis, you know. And then, father said, give me a job. What you doing tonight? Come on down. Be down there at eight o'clock. I'll be down there. Well, they go wherever they got to go, they'll leave me, you know. I'll play for them. They'll come and give me a dollar, six, you know. Finally, I got sold, I began to hire me. That's a hard story. Looking back and I began to doing pretty good.
Did you get any, belonged to any regular band then pretty soon? Oh yeah.

Yeah. I used to see, Jimmy and this boy was playing with the Imphil band, you see. Manuel. Manuel. Perez. Perez. He was kind of sickly, I think he had an ulcer in his stomach. Kind of sickly all the time. I used to play right regular with Manuel. And that's a Jimmy Brown. Yeah, and at that time, George Ybarquet was playing. Clionette, Manuel Sumpet. Buddy Johnson? Buddy Johnson, no. George Field. George Field. He played some boom. And this boy Nick. Henry Nickerson. Henry Nickerson was playing violin. Yeah.
I don't know much about him. Was he ever, any relation to Professor Nickerson? His son. Oh, it's his son. Yeah, I told you about it.
He had a sister named Camille.
Camille. So violin that Johnny has then was to be for him.

That's one of the sons. He stayed on the corner and the room. Well, Henry did. Henry did. But the father lived back in Galvin Canal. But after he got to playing violin, then he got away from home. Yeah. The old man didn't want him in no band. He didn't want him. All that bunch of old ladies and the old man up on him when he got into that imperial band. He was kind of sickly anyhow. Yeah, kind of sickly father. And they didn't want him. He was like this boy Benny Raphael. Wonderful trombone, young trombone player. Yes, he was. Stared down on Claiborne and Calorite. He was, I mean, he was a good trombone player. Died early. Died early. He didn't drink nothing but tea. Come to the house, make him a pot of tea, a cup of tea.
Do you remember about what years you played with the imperial band?

I guess I could. That's how I come together with Ori, playing with the imperial band. George Fields, they said, they got a young fella just come here from Mountain or Plats, Louisiana, named Ori. And he said, they got a little band. He said, you be just a guy for them guys. He said, they need a bass man. He said, go on down there and help them out. Join them. Play with them, help them out. He said, I think they got something. And that's true for me how they have them. George Fields, trombone man. And they sitting on the bandstand, he told me. I said, well I'll go by there and see him. And at that time, his brother Johnny Ori had a saloon at Conine and Claiborne. Is that the same brother that had the chicken farm out there?
Yeah. I never did meet him.
He died. Johnny Ori. Yeah. Johnny Ori. So, uh.
He had a saloon down there down there.
So I went on down there to meet him.
Where was that saloon? Cleaborn and Coni.
Right on the corner, yeah. Almost in the district, wasn't he? Yeah.
Just two blocks different. Yeah.

I was saying, Robinson, Virick, Gass, and Elmery. So you joined Ori then? So I went down there and talked to Ori and Ori. That's because I come to the Royce and I went on to the Royce and I went on to the Royce and I never knew the tunes they were playing because there wasn't enough but to make up tunes out there in the country, you know. Oh, yeah. Like the 1919 and all that, you know.
Oh, yeah.

Well, I played with him and I said, oh, man, can't you stay with us? I said, well, I'll think about it. You know, I was particular. Because you know, I'd be down, down, down, down, in the red light, you know, and around this ship. Finally, I said, alright. I stayed with him. And that's how it happened. That's great. Them guys used to get a deposit on the job and everybody get, they had everybody something but be, because I never wanted to. I said, give it to them boys. I didn't, you know. And lots of times we'd get, we'd get messed up, we'd get all our money and I didn't get nothing but they would, you know. Yeah. I said, well, let them have it, it's alright. And me and Johnny Dots fight every night. Every night. What about? Every night we'd have a fight. What about?
Over the music or something? Yeah, over the music, anything.
Just start an argument. Just that Montutti business. You know, he laugh all the time.
Montutti.

He'd laugh, you know. I'd walk all the way and Johnny Dots in the mouth. There we'd start, he'd grab me, you know, me and him. Homes would be falling over, me and everything else. Get up, brush off, call the plane and we'd come on out there and he'd think we'd never had no trouble at all. Walking on, nobody'd ride because we couldn't get on the streetcar every time. Yeah, with the days. And we'd be just walking and talking, you know. And forgot about it, we had to fight. Next night, fight again. Yeah. Don't nobody in the theater. Not an out-fired though, I think.
I've heard that you all played mostly with Oregon.

Well, most during that time, when Oregon really began to get to know. We used to play lots of time out in the country, you know. Every play there was St. John, Lake Charles, Donisonville, you know. We used to play over here. We had a place to play in, uh. There was Coles Lawn. Oh, we was there for years at Coles Lawn. Coles Lawn. Jackson, Will and Puff. Played Coles Lawn and played St. Couches. We played all over there. We just kept down at the Tulane University. Those boys, a lot. They got right popular around there. Can you tell us a bit more about Miss Coles Lawn parties, or what it was like? Yeah, yeah. She runs Saturday and Sunday, all holidays. And, uh, it used to be packed in there.
Uh, she was crazy about the band.

She always said if she'd ever die, she'd want that band to play at her funeral. Mm-hmm. And, uh, it used to be packed in there. Uh, she was crazy about the band. She always said if she'd ever die, she'd want that band to play at her funeral. Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm .
Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm .
Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm .
Mm-hmm .
Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . I wasn't there, no I. I wasn't there.
Did they charge to get in for those parties?
Oh yeah, fifty cents. Sure.
And when they danced, was it right on the ground?
No, in a big pavilion, in a hall, you know.
It started to build up then, like a hall. Yeah. Well, I thought it was a long party.

But you had a long party in the yard once. The long party used to be at Third and Woola, on the lot where the baseball team was. That's where long parties used to be. We used to have two bands sometimes playing out there. Right in that big lot, we used to play baseball. Third and Woola. They named it the National Park once. Yeah, yeah. Yeah, they fenced it in, you know. They had boxing, they had boxing there because Harry Wells and George Smith fought there. They had lawns right in there.
And this pavilion that she built, was that down at her home or?
Yeah, she lived somewhere on the side there somewhere, back in there somewhere.
Yeah. Because there's still an old house there at Willow and Josephine, but I didn't know.
No, this was in the back and there was an old pavilion. In the back, so.
Yeah. They served drinks or food? Sure. They didn't all there.
Beer.
Yeah. Beer. Most of the people had left the back. Beer and food, you know.
Mm-hmm. That beer and that food.
Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm .
Mm-hmm .
Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm .
Mm-hmm . and this band comes to me and wants a band to go to Chicago and we're going to travel. We're going to take Freddie Kepert's place, Mabel, Elaine and the New Orleans Jazz Band.
Oh yes.

You remember that? The first time the first bunch went away was Freddie, George Dibacque, Jimmy Pollard, a bunch like that. Eddie Benson. Eddie Benson went off to the next group. Who else went? Another group went because they're taking Cantrell. Another group went was Cantrell, Eddie Atkins. Yeah, that's right. And Manuel Perez. Manuel Perez, yeah, that's it. And Frankie Hain. Frankie Hain. And Teo. Lorraine Teo. Who was the Teo? Lil Cantrell. That's right. Then I, then I left and I was taking the group. I was taking Sugar Johnny. Trumpet. Trumpet. Lewis Kepert, guitar. Myself on bass. Lil Happy on drums. Herbert Lindsey on violin. Philip. Philip, yeah.
It was the trombone. Huh? The trombone. You remember?

Roy Pond. Roy Pond and the trombone. That was the band I had. And we got to Illinois, Illinois Central Station. And we just fixed to get on the train and this agent who was, you know, was taking care of the business on this end. Come up and said, just a minute, just got a telegram. Cut the drum out. Poor Happy like the fellow out there. Yeah. So Red Happy? Red Happy? You know what happened to the drummer? Just picking up his drum fish to get up on there. Yeah. On the steps, you know, on the train. And the man coming. Tori. Got to cancel you. What happened, man? Jesus come out there. And I wanted to get away. I didn't care. I'm so glad. And we come on Chicago. The agent book and agent with Lee Krause. And don't forget it. And then I come down there on, where was he? Down on Jackson and the Wabash up on the 10th and 11th floor. We rehearse around there. And Mabel, he laid in the white girl. She make a black face. And she's dancing in wooden shoes like Bo Jiggins.
Oh, yeah.

Yeah, Bill Robinson. And a big bale of cottons on the stage, right in the center stage. And she's in this bale of cottons. And when we start to play, that bale of cottons just open up like that. And she come out. And she's there. Oh, she could go. Oh, they had us on. We had beautiful cover halls, you know, different colors.
Is that the one that had the steamboat? Yeah, it's better. Is Lawrence Dewey the... Lawrence Dewey was the carnet band. Yeah, I've seen that picture.
Yeah.
That was about 1912, you say. Was it that early?
Yeah, around 1912 or 19... Yeah, 1912.
When you left the island, is that right? Yeah. Right to Chicago. Where did you play? In theaters?
In theaters, so I traveled all around.
All over the country.

I traveled all around. Yeah. And then I come back, you know, and I got a job. Well, we went over in Chicago, such as Blue Monday, Blue Wednesday, Blue Tuesday, the Dreamland and have it on Mondays. DeLux would have it on Tuesdays, T9 Jones, number two, like, different days. And all the entertainers would go from one place to another. So we went on, they invited us to come over to the DeLux. I was upstairs over to Old Panama's, right Old Panama Club. It's been 35th and State. I went up there and playing, everybody was crazy about it. In the Orleans Jazz Band, I was during that time slapping bass, all the hornets around me like that, you know. Yeah.
There's something new to that.

Yeah, so. So Shaw said, how would you like to work up there? How would you like your band up there? I said, all right. He said, all right, I'll give you a job. I said, okay. Well, it didn't belong to the Union. Well, we played there a couple of weeks, you know. Finally, the cards kept coming there. Well, they had three men playing there. They played for the entertainers. Cora, Cora, Caroline Williams, Florence Mills, Brick Top, Cora Williams, and another girl, Justine, this Justine girl. They played for the entertainers. These three fellas, clarinet, piano, and drums. They came out and said, you fellas belong to the Union, I'll have to get the Union. I said, who? I'll get no Union. I know it's get the Union, you're going to freeze me out. That's what you know. I'll have to do Union. I said, no, no, nobody can freeze you out. You got your band to freeze you out for what? I said, oh, no. I said, oh, I'm telling you, you got John's Union. Everybody's Union here and you all can't play here. Finally, old Copeland come down, the secretary, one day. I said, who's the leader? All that girls. They said, you boys will have to come on in, take out a card. I said, well, take out a card for what? Well, I want to be in Union. I got my own group. He said, that's all right, but you're working in the Union house. And everything was Union. Waiters in the hall was Union in there. Oh, I couldn't see it. He said, well, all right. He said, if you boys don't join the Union, he told Mr. Shaw, he says, we'll have to pull these other boys out of here and we're going to pull these waiters. So Mr. Shaw comes to me and he said, that night, he said, you done have me to check out. Give me a check. Just take this down to Union and take your boys down. I said, I don't join them. They're going to mess it. They ain't going to mess up. You're working here for me. They say, you got the Johnny Union. Just take that and just go on down there. That's how I got in the Union. Shaw gave me the check and made the band join the Union. And we joined the Union. And them guys used to hang around with Sugar Johnny, you know, poor sugar. He had Sugar Johnny blow, you know. And then I stayed there quite a while. And then this fellow Nick Williams, George Williams, opened up the club on 34th Street. It was called, what do you call that club? He named the tune after it.
It was called the Royal Garden.

Royal Garden. And he wants some music, you know. Well, I said, it's a good chance for us to get our old band together. I said, yeah, I'll send for Joe Oliver. Can you get him? I said, sure, I can get him. All right, I'll send for Joe Oliver. That's Joe Oliver. Johnny Dodds come in with Mac and Mac. Over to this little old theater. They had a little old theater there on State Street. It's your big time, you know. He was in there.
Mutt was living for a while too. Mac was there.

I mean, Mutt was there. Yeah. Yeah. I still, I still, uh, may share. And Mutt said, I said, Mutt, I can get you John too. Mutt said, well, I'll go far to St. Louis and I'll jump at St. Louis. He left with St. Louis, but, oh, Bessier just left right away. Well, he played up the deluxe with me. He decided, what's doing? Mutt come back. See? Well, I got Mutt with me. Johnny was very sick, you know. He was sick, you know. I was there. He stayed with me. Then I got Joe. Finally, Nora Dutrae comes through town. He's running a ship. You know, a sailor. Used to come in, you know, and come and sit in and play. So he's telling us about his time was going to go. He'd be off. Be out in the Navy. Nora got out the Navy. We got Nora. Then finally, Minor Hall come in town. Running on the Southern Pacific. Dishwasher over. Why didn't he? He come in town. His mother would live in Chicago and his brother, Tubby. He went to the Army. No, he didn't. No, we got him before he went to the Army. Yeah. He come in town. We got a hold of him. Then we organized our regular bunch. So that name, and I got a girl named Lil Harden. It's the name of Lil Armstrong. She was working for Mrs. Jones, selling music and demonstrating it to the people, you know. And I needed a piano player. I was going to play on the west side for the Chinese, George, you know, at a cafe. But they wanted piano. I had Louis playing guitar. Louis Kaplan. Yeah. So I said, I'm going to get this girl. You know, she could play. I know she could play. So I asked her, I said, I would like to play a job. You want to play a gig tonight with her? Yeah, I'll play with you. I said, brother, you know. I don't know what it's paid. I'll play. She just wanted to be with the jazz. Say she was in a jazz band. That's the only jazz band. So she said, you ask Mrs. Jones. I said, Mrs. Jones, can I use your piano player? Now listen. Listen, you come in here to steal. I said, steal your piano player. I just want to use it tonight. All right. We started the monkey business. I said, how can it be monkey business? I ain't got no regular job. I'm just going down there to play this gig. All right. She can go. Okay. We went down there to Charmin hard the band. She liked the band. And she was, oh, you know how old she was? 17 years old. That's old. That's right. I put her in a place of band. And I went down there and play and she used to go home. And I said, well, where are you? Where are you at all the time? Well, she was playing down at the church. She lied to her mother for years. Said she was at some church.
She was playing at some church. She was playing at the...

And we all got together playing in the dreamlands. She still thought she was playing at some church or something. And her mother come and they caught her. Too late then. And Miss Jones gave me the devil. I said, I know you're going to steal my girl. I didn't. Soon she went out. I know that was the last of it. She went down and played that day and didn't go back tomorrow. Called Miss Jones up and said, I got a regular job with that band.
And I'm going to live this woman's house. I live at Miss Jones's house.
She said, I know you're going to do that, you devil. And she's crazy about the band, on the old man's boat. Right.
Where was that store?
On the state in the 33rd, the 34th.
Oh yeah.
They used to book bands and they used to send people on jobs, you know. Yeah, in private. So you see, they'd send you on jobs.
Yeah.

That's pretty good. And I went on over and I got Joe, then we organized the band. So we had Joe Oliver, Nora Dutre. Well first we had Roy before Nora come back. We had Roy, Joe, Johnny Dodge, Ram, it's mine and all, myself, and Lil. Who else? Who else? That's all. That's all. Joe, Leo, Miner, Roy Palmer, myself, and the piano players. That was six years.
You said Lil' Kepard's were wanting to play guitar.
Guitar, yeah. Then after that, you know. No guitar.
No.
They didn't want no guitar. They want piano.
Yeah.
You know, we left home, we were playing the piano, we were playing the guitar. Yeah, yeah. The piano down in the Storyville, you know. Oh man.

Well I was going to ask one more question about that first band on that show, you know, with Mamie Lane and all. What kind of music did you play? Did you just play for her singing or did you play other pieces too?

Yeah, we had a regular routine, yeah. We had, she had numbers that we played for her to dance by, you know. And we used to play roles, not rolling, we used to play on the Rowdy League. Oh yeah, Rowdy League. Yeah, we played that, she used to dance that. Then we had a couple of band numbers we done, you see.
Some of the New Orleans numbers?
Yeah, yeah. Standard numbers. Yeah, yeah, that's right, yeah. Pretty good it was too.
And that first job done in the Chicago, the Chinese restroom, is that on sort of the west side?

I was over on the west side, yeah. I was over on, I think I was over on Madison. I was over on Madison, some left in there, Palina, Madison Palina. And we all played up there, Madison Palina, at the Sonia with myself, Emmanuel Perez, Teo, Lorenzo Teo, Cantrell, Frank Aime, and Dixieland, and the only Dixieland band was the other. The original five. There was in one corner and there was the other corner.
That was the Ansonia.
The Ansonia, yeah. There was one corner and there was the other corner.
You played with that band for a while then too, with Manuel?
Yeah. Then when they come back, we left there, then I had Manuel with me over in the Deluxe. Then I had a job playing down at the Pekin. That's 28th and the State. Yeah. It was an old Pekin Theater.
They tore it down finally. It was a police station.
Police station, yeah.
Then they tore it down about four or five years ago. They tore it down? A big housing project. Yeah.

So we played down there after we leave the Dreamland. We'd go down to Pekin and stay there until four or five o'clock in the morning. We had a good band down there. Dan Jackson. I had that job. Dan Jackson was running old Mott Brunelaw. It was his father-in-law, brother. Man Jackson married his daughter. Our son's for Charlie McCurdies. He played in the theater and I had him to play, I believe, the theater down there too. He and Theo together on the clarinet. Charlie disappeared. Nobody ain't never know the day where Charlie went out. He just went out. Is that right? I know. He was playing with Dave down there. You know, it was good. Crinet.
Dave Payton?
He was playing in the Grand Theater with Dave Payton and then he come on down there, you see. He just disappeared. Nobody ain't never know where that fellow went out.
Well, I remember once, the only time I ever talked to Emmanuel Perez, he said that when they sent for McCurdy or something that he was pretty old and didn't do so well and the...
And that one I sent for him, he said, yeah, he done all right. No, no.
And then they sent and had the Piku to come up and replace him.
Well, Piku never did come there. Not at the Grand Theater.
I don't know what that was then. Maybe Emmanuel had it wrong.
He had it wrong. That I knew.
Or a different place, different job.

That might be somewhere else. Yeah. He wasn't all that old. He wasn't all that old. No, he played like the devil. He was playing that for Dave Payton. Dave was crazy about it. Okay. And at that time, these fellas was using the A and the B. And he didn't use nothing but that B. Transposed.
Transposed, yeah. Do you remember Fess if he ever came back to New Orleans later or died there or anything? Who was that? McCurdy?
He came back. He came back and he lived at Jones' house. John Rovershire.
John Rovershire. And he died there in the city then? Oh, he did? You remember?
He was dead a long time. Not John, I mean the Cush. John McCurdy was dead a long time, sir. Yeah.
And when he died, sir. Because he just skipped out of Chicago and never heard from him up there.
Oh, he lived many years after he got out of Chicago during the time I knew. Oh, yeah. Yeah.
Well, then when did you go to Royal Garden? Was that before or after the uh-

Oh, no. Joe went over to Royal Garden and I was at the Dreamland. Then Joe left and come join us at there. Then I turned the band over to Joe. See? At the Dreamland. Then we left the Dreamland to come to the Pecola Dance Hall on Market Street.
Where?
In San Francisco. In San Francisco.
Yeah.

And that was in 1921. We left Chicago May the 30th that morning. I got out of the morning. May the 30th. Hot as a storm we got. Mm-hmm. And he come on that north west, the great north west, and we're staying. Yeah. Until the first go. I think it would take about four days to get you that time. Yeah.
How long did you stay at that dance hall? Do you remember about?
Yeah, we stayed there. Oh, we stayed there quite a while.
In December weeks anyway. Almost. It wasn't a year though, I guess.
No, no, no. What happened after we got there, we had David Jones playing a mellophone.
Oh, yeah.

And he could execute on a mellophone as fast as John Dots could on his clarinet. And he played an alto sax too. Well, we was playing there and Jimmy Pilar was playing violin and doubling on his beat tenor, you know, tenor saxophone, Nora on trombone, Lil on piano, myself on bass, Joe, and around minor hall. So something come up and he wanted to do away with Jimmy. See, Jimmy Pilar. Yeah. And finally he was going to let Jimmy Pilar go and so minor taking it up. Minor say, a man come all the way out there to the end of the sudden surface. He said, why are you talking about you're going to let the man go? He said, well, if you're going to do that, let me go. I'll go too. Well, the big stick come up so they went to the union, reported to the union. Well, at that time, Joe jumps up and sends for Baby Dodge. Baby Dodge was in St. Louis. He sends for Baby Dodge without going and get privilege from the union. Joe didn't know he had to go to the union, you know, find out if he could invoke somebody into San Francisco. Well, when they called Joe up, then they had me to come up. He asked Joe, he said, who gave you permission to send for this man? I said, nobody. He said, nobody. I said, no, you're wrong. He said, why didn't you come to the union? I said, no. They said, do you know if this man is a financier in the union, in good standard? He says, I don't know. No, no. He said, well, he's not. They were suspended or something. All right. He says, did you get Mr. Palau's notice, a written notice? No, I was told. He said, you either pay him two weeks, or you have to wait two weeks, give him two weeks. He says, and the drummer, say he'd quit too. He said, did they give you a notice? He says, no. He said, he's got the right two weeks. If you want to leave or you want him to leave, you got to pay him too. He had to pay Johnny Dodd, I mean, and Jimmy Palau.
He said, what's up?

Well, they fined Joe $250. See? Joe jumped up and went to pay it, and when we closed there, Joe hadn't paid it. He went away, and he got the man. And I stayed. I wouldn't go back. All of them went back but me. See, Ram's and quit, but Baby Dodds was there. They all went back. I wouldn't go. I stayed. I stayed. And he goes to New York or somewhere. He had then about a 12-piece band. He had a guy. Yeah. See, Bill Johnson take my place.
I started Bill Johnson. So you stayed out here then? Yeah. And who'd you work with then?

Over there, because that's where I was going. Nowhere was here, I was always over there. Over there in Oakland. He went to work. He went to work. And he goes to work at where this place was at 35th and Calumet. Oh yeah. Where Al-Twenty's old place was. That's where they built the cage. The cage? The cage? What is it? Yeah, I forgot the name. A big place there.
Plantation.
And they called it Plantation. That's it.
Plantation. That's it.

And they found Joe there. And Joe, they found everybody. A hundred, all the players was with him. One hundred dollars a piece. And they put two hundred and fifty dollars more on Joe. And it all had to be paid that night or he couldn't hit a tap. And some woman, you know what I told me? I went and bought a tub. I said, this woman wrote out a check and paid us for Joe. Yeah. He had about twelve or thirteen in the band.
Yeah, a big band.

He had Donnell Howard on it. Yeah. Clionette, Barney Biggar, Nick. Nick, you know Nick. Clionette, Albert. Had them three guys on Clionette. And Tennant, they all played Tennant. Well, you know, that's what they called. He paid about a thousand dollars there. And they couldn't hit a tap. And they called him where it was loaded. And the man walked up there and said, I'm sorry. He'd have paid us right now.
You stayed out here and there.
I've been right here.
And worked in the...
I went on right there in Midori. And we went to work for Mike Lyman down on Spring Street.
Oh, here in the old thing.
On Spring years ago, yeah. And we left there. And I went right out in the J's room or that was where he is.
Oh yeah, I remember that.
But we was playing at the plantation out in Culver City. He built a place out there, a beautiful place. And I went to the J's room.
Oh, do you remember... No, you weren't here when Jelly Roll was out here, I guess, much.
At Leakes Lake. Sure. Where are you here? I played around here with Jelly Roll. That's right.
He was here then. You weren't here though when Buddy Petit and Frankie Dusen came out, were you?

Oh, Frankie Petit. Yeah, Frankie was here. I come in here. I come in here. It wasn't long. I come right in here when it is. There wasn't over... I was here for a couple of weeks. I used to go see Freddie was over at the Red Onion, Buddy Petit was playing over there. And Frankie was... Ding Johnson. See, Ding Johnson sent from. It was playing. That was right there at 10th and Central.
The Red Onion was 10th and Central. Yeah.
And Buddy Petit was over there.

Right. And that's it. The Cadillac was down on 5th... Down on 4th Street. 4th Street. 4th and Central. That's right. Do you remember, were you on those records, those first records that already made in 1921? The Sunshine. Yeah. Can you remember anything about that date? Sure.

I'm sure. The first record he ever made, I was right there with him. And during that time, it wasn't recording. The bass didn't record, you see. The drum didn't record. The drummer had to set up a symbol up on the table and a wood block. It'd be on a wood block and hit the symbol. That's all it would record. But my bass didn't record. That was too long. Or bass drum wouldn't record.
That was too long.
That was funny. That was funny.
How come they got Dink on that date to play clarinet? Do you remember?
Yeah. Well, I don't know what happened to Wade, you see.
Wade had been with you all that time?
Yeah. But we got Dink. Wills and Spice had to go Dink. I don't know. Something. I don't know. We got a hold of him. I don't know.
Well, they did one of Dink's tunes too. That was the Ticket Blues. Yeah.
Then we played our oldest Creole trombone, you see. Then Someday Sweetheart.
Where were those records made? Which?
We out there in Santa Monica. Out on Pico Street there.
Way up.
Yeah. Little old funny place. They were Spice Brothers, you know. And Alberta, Alberta, she sang one song and this other girl sang. Ruth somebody. Ruth, Ruth, yeah. Ruth and Alberta, yeah.
It might have been Ruth Lee or something like that. That doesn't sound good. Yeah.
Well, they sang. They were doing the singing.
You never recorded with King Oliver, I guess, any time? No, I didn't get it.

No, I left, you see. That's what he was going to do because he wanted to go to New York. I told him I ain't going to go to New York. I'm going to stay here. I get my shoes shined the whole year around in California.
Yeah.
I ain't got your car and I ain't got your California woman. I ain't leaving. I said, yeah, I'm going to stay here. Yeah. All right.
Your wife came from Chicago, I believe she said the other day. When were you married? Yeah.
She comes to Chicago. That's right.
When were you married? No.
Oh, I don't know. But I didn't, I didn't, I didn't, not in Chicago here. It was over, out here. Out here, yeah, in 1927.
So you came here in about 1921 and then in the state?
I come down in 21 states, yeah. No, 21, I come down, yeah, in 21 and I went back to Oakland, played around there. But I come back to Oakland, but I come back to the state.
Yeah. Yeah. I wonder if you could tell us a little bit about the bass, what you, when did you learn to read? You say you started out without learning to read.
Yeah, I started out with faking, yeah. A little reading I'd done, a little learning I got. I started at Dave, at Old Man Jackson. Yeah.
Had anybody, uh, 34 years in there. Had anybody given you any lessons at all, even about playing the bass in New Orleans?
Oh yeah, sure, oh, I got a lot of, a lot of lessons, um, I got a lot of ideas from real good bass players. Like I told you, this Henry Kimmel. Yeah. He actually showed you the thing rings.
He actually showed you the thing rings to read him.
He said, Dave, listen. Yeah, he's a thing ring. He showed me how to use this. E string, which I know he'd use before. I take it off, but it was in my way. Too many strings.
But he didn't teach you to read them?

No, he just teached me the fingerboard, you know, and I went on. And, uh, lots of different bass players, older bass players than I was, more experienced than I was, give me a lot of ideas, showed me, you know.
Well, can you tell me, in the old days, did they pick mostly four beats to the major, or maybe just two beats? I told them. Well, no. Faster or slower than they did.
Yeah. And most of them, in the old days, we'd done most of our four beats. We'd be the two beats, then four, then what we call, so let's double it up. That's what we should call doubling up.
Yeah.
See? That's why that four beats come in. We'd be playing. Let's double up. That's why that four beats, they start that four beats. Yeah. And we start that. You know, syncopation.
How is this? I've even heard you double up where it sounds like you're hitting an 8. I don't know. What do you do? Just pick real fast or do you let it snap or what goes on?
When you make them full beats?
Sometimes it sounds like you make an 8 to the measure when you go so fast. Well you're doubling up on them. Yeah, how do you double that? Do you just pick it faster?

You see, you're fingering too. Yeah, you can pick. The way you hit it, let it go, you understand? Yeah. Pull it, let it go to your finger and make that sound come from your fingers. Bip-bump, bip-bump.
Oh yeah, with your left hand fingers sometimes.
Bip-bump, yeah. Bip-bump, bimp. See, it's like going to hit it, choke it, you know. Yeah. Bip-bump, bump.
Yeah. Done a lot of that in the left hand too. Yeah.
Not done anything real fast.
Yeah. When you pick, do you try to let the strings snap back against the fingerboard?
Well, you used to do it. Not no more now. Don't like that. No. You see, it's like a record. You can't do that.
No.
Cause it makes too much noise. You understand. slap your fingerboard hitting it. Pap, pap, pap. No, I'm fine. No, I don't hit the fingerboard at all, no. You get a true tone out of your enderman.
When you're gonna talk about the slap bass.
Nah, that hits the fingerboard. Does that mean you actually slap it
with your hip hard enough?
Yeah, bump, bump, bump, bump, bump, bump, bump, bump. You know, bump, bump, bump, bump. You hit the fingerboard, bump, bump, bump, pull on the strings, back.
Then you pick it as you go away. Yeah, pull it back, slap it in. Slap it against the fingerboard.
That's right. That's it.
When you were young and practiced on your bass, or did you ever practice at home, or just mostly on the job? Did you ever get?
Well, when I used to be around home, I used to practice around home.
What would you practice on, things like scales? Scales. Or pieces?
Scales. Yeah, I used to practice, I tell you a lot of things I used to practice. I used to practice a lot of solos. I liked solos.
Mm-hmm. Where you'd actually play the melody, or?
Oh, I played a lot of that stuff on my bass.
I remember on the blues, that blues for Jimmy, you'd play something that comes from,

like, Stanford Lucia, don't you? Part of it, part of it is on the road of Jerusalem. Oh yeah. That sounds like Jerusalem, part of Jerusalem. Oh yeah. The Holy City they'd call it. Oh yeah. The Holy City. You used to play that on the violin. Yeah. Oh yeah. The Holy City. You used to play that on the violin. Yeah. And those things you always bow on those.
I bow, yeah, I bow. I play a lot of stuff where I bow.
I play a lot of stuff where I bow. I just sing a close walk with me.
Oh yes, I've heard that.
I play that with solo on my bass.
Da.
When you bow, how do you hold the bow? Do you hold it like that or this way?
See, yeah, that's it. I think they bow like the German style. French style. French style. French style.
It's like that. Yeah. That's the correct way.
That's the correct way.
But do you ever put your fingers in the bow? Yeah, that's it. That's it.
I have a good bass.
Have you ever used any of those aluminum basses or tried one of those?

No, I played on those. I don't want one. No, they ain't no good. You don't like the tone? Ain't nobody. It's how long they last. They don't last, do you? You crack them or not crack them, down them, you understand? And no tone out of them.
How long have you had your instrument, the one you have now?
The one I got now I had since 19... Yeah, I had this instrument since 19... about this one, 1921.
1921, huh? Do you know what kind it is, if it's French or German or Italian or American or whatever it is made?
That bass is made in Switzerland.
Made in Switzerland?

And the name of it, I got the name, I forgets it every time a man told that bass rules and told me, you keep this in your mind. Uh-huh. They said, good bass, that's something like a German bass, you know?
Yeah, where did you buy it then?
I got that bass, I bought that bass during the Time War Line, not War Line, no way in the audience. I bought that bass from Broadway and 5th, between...

Oh, here in Los Angeles? Los Angeles, yeah. Yeah. Um... Sherman and Clague. Sherman and Clague, oh, yeah, they have a big store up in San Francisco. Yeah. There's an odd one here now. Oh, yeah, I've already been in that one. I guess they have them all over the West. Um... Well... ... ... ... ... ... ... ... ... ... ...
I was wondering what other things you practiced on, if you ever practiced on any other extra finger exercises or different...
Oh yeah, I don't know, scales, yeah, scales, you know. I don't know, keep your finger in fit.
Yeah.
Yeah. See, that was a cross-the-board exercise. You practice so? Then you take whole notes, you know.
Yeah.
Whole notes.
You go back, you see? I wondered if you had any suggestions about taking care of the bass or in traffic?

segments.title: Opening and identification
segments.summary: Garland asks what to talk about and gives his name.

segments.title: Birthplace on Basin Street and the Montudie nickname
segments.summary: Born January 9, 1895 near the old Parish prison; he explains how bandmates teased him with the nickname Montutti until it stuck.

segments.title: Older brother John Garland and his instruments
segments.summary: His older brother John, now ill in Philadelphia, played violin, trombone, mandolin and guitar; only he and Ed survive.

segments.title: Parents and church music as a boy
segments.summary: His mother died when he was about four; he attended St. James Methodist church with friends while also going to the Catholic church.

segments.title: Earliest bands he heard: the Imperial Band
segments.summary: He recalls brass bands and orchestras in his youth, especially the Imperial Band and bassist Jimmy Brown.

segments.title: First instruments and learning to read in Chicago
segments.summary: He started on guitar and mandolin with his brother, settled on bass, had no lessons until Chicago and studied with Dave Jackson.

segments.title: Three-string bass, Henry Kimball and homemade bowing
segments.summary: At about ten he played his brother's three-string bass, learned a four-string bass from Henry Kimball, and made rosined thread bows.

segments.title: How pizzicato and slap bass came about
segments.summary: He says nobody knew who first plucked; players broke bows, picked, and slap bass developed from that.

segments.title: Favorite old-time bass players
segments.summary: He names Sam Nixon, Henry Kimball and Jimmy Brown as good bassists.

segments.title: Jimmy Johnson, Bolden and Kenny's Hall
segments.summary: He covers Jimmy Johnson, who played with Bolden, Jack Carey and the Crescent Band, and substituting for him at Kenny's Hall, a dance hall used as a church on Sundays, with that band's lineup.

segments.title: His first job at a house party
segments.summary: At about nine or ten he played bass at a house party with his brother and Caniniis Jackson and fell asleep on the bandstand.

segments.title: Playing with Manuel Perez and the Imperial band
segments.summary: He played regularly with Manuel Perez's group alongside George Fields and Henry Nickerson, whose father disapproved of his playing.

segments.title: Joining Ory's band
segments.summary: George Fields sent him to the new young Ory, whose brother Johnny had a saloon; he joined despite not knowing their country tunes, and fought nightly with Johnny Dodds over the nickname.

segments.title: Ory's band at Coles Lawn and country dates
segments.summary: The band played country towns and Coles Lawn, a pavilion with a woman owner who loved them; he also describes the ballpark lot at Third and Willow.

segments.title: Leaving for Chicago with the New Orleans Jazz Band and Mabel Elaine
segments.summary: Several New Orleans groups went north; Ed led one, lost his drummer at the station, and toured theaters in Chicago with Mabel Elaine's act around 1912.

segments.title: Playing the DeLux in Chicago and joining the union
segments.summary: His band played at the DeLux on 35th and State and was forced into the union by the owner after union pressure.

segments.title: Assembling the Oliver band and hiring Lil Hardin
segments.summary: For the Royal Garden he recruited Joe Oliver, Johnny Dodds, Mutt Carey, Norah, Minor Hall, and borrowed pianist Lil Hardin from Mrs. Jones's music store.

segments.title: Booking at the music store and the band's lineup
segments.summary: The store booked bands; he lists the band he put together with Oliver and notes that the piano replaced the guitar.

segments.title: Repertoire for Mabel's show
segments.summary: The group played routines for her dance and some standard numbers.

segments.title: West side jobs and the Ansonia with Perez
segments.summary: He recalls the Chinese restaurant job and Madison Street, and the Ansonia with Perez, Teo, Cantrell and Frank Aime.

segments.title: The Pekin and Charlie McCurdy
segments.summary: After the Dreamland they played the Pekin until morning; he recalls McCurdy's disappearance, Piku and Dave Payton's band.

segments.title: Leaving Dreamland for San Francisco in 1921
segments.summary: Oliver went to the Royal Garden, then the band moved to the Pecola dance hall in San Francisco, leaving Chicago May 30, 1921.

segments.title: Union fine over Baby Dodds and Ed staying on the coast
segments.summary: Oliver sent for Baby Dodds without union permission, was fined $250, and Ed stayed behind while the others returned.

segments.title: The Plantation club and Oliver's big band
segments.summary: He describes the Plantation and Oliver's dozen-piece band stranded for payment.

segments.title: Los Angeles work and Jelly Roll, Buddy Petit
segments.summary: He worked for Mike Lyman and the Plantation in Culver City, played around with Jelly Roll, and saw Buddy Petit at the Red Onion.

segments.title: The 1921 Los Angeles recordings
segments.summary: He recalls the first record date in Santa Monica where his bass and bass drum did not record, Dink on clarinet, and singers Ruth and Alberta.

segments.title: Staying in California and marriage
segments.summary: He refused to go to New York with Oliver and married in California in 1927.

segments.title: Learning to read and bass lessons
segments.summary: He faked at first, got some reading from Dave Jackson, and got ideas and fingerboard instruction from older bassists.

segments.title: Two beats, four beats and doubling up
segments.summary: He explains how old bands doubled up from two to four beats and how left-hand fingering produces fast notes.

segments.title: Slap bass technique
segments.summary: He describes slapping the strings against the fingerboard, which does not suit records.

segments.title: Practice and solos on bass
segments.summary: He practiced scales and solos, including Holy City and Walk With Me, bowed.

segments.title: Bow grip
segments.summary: He says he uses French style bow grip.

segments.title: His bass and aluminum basses
segments.summary: He dislikes aluminum basses; his own Swiss-made bass was bought in Los Angeles around 1921.

segments.title: Practice exercises and closing question
segments.summary: He mentions scales and whole notes for keeping fingers fit; the interviewer asks about caring for the bass.
